02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.name: Bowl (*Sakızlık*)
02992f2b-3701-5bc3-ba32-d5f6226b56ef.short_description: From historical sources, we learn that vessels made of gold and silver were widely used in the Ottoman palace. Starting from the end of the 18th century, Baroque and Rococo forms of Western style replaced classical Ottoman designs. We find roses in relief, the Ottoman coat-of-arms, architectural compositions, casted flowers, birds and animals on a multitude of the vessels of the era. This cylindrical cup with pedestal foot and cupola-like hinged lid was made of vermeil silver. On the body of the cup we see a floral pattern and hanging lambs placed alternatingly. Flowers, buds and leaves are made from rubies and diamonds nailed into gold and silver contours. On the lid – instead of lamb motif on the body – a chalice was used. The foot of the chalice is in the form of a cherub from which a bundle of rays projects.

0f2fd351-f23b-5e56-9d5a-58ba529c43c4.name: Emerald-covered box
0f2fd351-f23b-5e56-9d5a-58ba529c43c4.short_description:
This spectacular gold box has a circular base, vertical sides and a low domed lid. 103 emeralds have been set in the 16 slightly convex rectangular panels of the sides and the 16 curving triangular sections that form the lid. The side panels are carved in shallow relief with cypress trees, their tips curving to the left; the same motif is repeated in the panels on the lid, but the tips of the trees are not curved. Narrow bands of gold frame the emerald panels and a 24-facet diamond is set at the apex of the lid. The base is covered with translucent green enamel and decorated with a central rosette and split acanthus leaves and palmettes.  
Emeralds were mined in Spanish Colombia, exported to Europe and then sent to Ottoman Turkey and Mughal India. Boxes of this type often had a matching tray and they could be used to hold medicines (including opium) or even more precious objects. They are featured in Mughal and Rajput miniature paintings from the end of the 16th century onwards.

117e4311-5f29-5b99-9692-18b2ed19cd70.short_description: The handle of this sabre is set with ivory, the crossguard with large sapphires and emeralds; the blade is decorated with gilt engraved etchings that contain the year AD 1813 and the name of Fath Ali (AD 1797–1834), the then reigning Shah. Perhaps the sword was presented to Emperor Franz I of Austria (AD 1768–1835) that year in an attempt to build a new alliance with Austria as a counterweight to Russia.

1339038e-f661-5345-9923-697aa6a4fa79.name: Oval amulet with Sura
1339038e-f661-5345-9923-697aa6a4fa79.short_description:
An oval amulet made of white and red garnet, with an inscribed invocation in the centre, framed by two lines. This is surrounded by *naskhi* epigraphy of *Surat Al-Fatiha* (*The Opening*) reading: "In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. All the praises and thanks be to Allah, the Lord of the Alamin (mankind, jinn and all that exists). The Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. The Only Owner (and the Only Ruling Judge) of the Day of Resurrection. You (Alone) we worship, and You (Alone) we ask for help (for each and everything). Guide us to the Straight Way. The way of those on whom You have bestowed Your Grace, not (the way) of those who earned Your Anger, nor of those who went astray".  
This *Sura* is framed by four lines. The outermost field is inscribed with qur’anic epigraphy of *Surat Al-Kafirun* reading: "In the Name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful. Say (O Muhammad) to (O Al – Kafirun) disbelievers in Allah: I worship not that which you worship, Nor will you worship that which I worship, and I shall not worship that which you are worshipping, Nor will you worship that which I worship, To you be your religion, and to me my religion (Islamic Monotheism)".  
The background of all the inscriptions is decorated with three- and five-fold dots, while the external frame is formed of two.

13a08655-b9b9-5fec-ae88-c539a6b04792.short_description: This jade plaque once belonged the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan (r. AH 1037-68/ AD 1628-58). 178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.name: Processional Altar of St. John the Evangelist
178f74aa-fe42-524b-94f2-f5d4a1c1bd50.description:
A silver processional altar made at the beginning of the 18th century, which belonged to the Royal Monastery of Our Lady of Conception, and was used in the Procession of the Holy Sacrament in Beja. The social and religious significance of the Corpus Christi Day procession cannot be understated; it represents one of the greatest manifestations of the Portuguese Baroque, which once acknowledged, justifies the sumptuousness of some of the pieces used in these ceremonies. Traditionally, up until 1893, the altar was carried by farmers.  
Rectangular in shape, the *acroteria* (small bases placed at the four extremities) has a beaded edging, and four *albarradas* or ornamental vases, alternate with smaller jars in the middle. The entirety is covered with vegetable and scalloped-shell ornamentation, and St. James' crosses. The wooden carrying rods are also silver plated.  
The octagonal shaped pedestal stands over the main body, decorated with double scalloped-shell ornamentation, pear-shaped “tables” and St. James' crosses. There is also an octagonal platform with small jars placed at each corner of the pedestal.  
An iron column rises above the pedestal, covered with silk cloth embroidered with gold thread. It meets a gold and silver halo embellished with precious stones above which a gold and silver crown rests, also studded with precious stones. In the middle of the altarpiece, the Martyrdom of St. John the Evangelist is played out, the saint graphically shown immersed in boiling olive oil. The wooden effigy of the saint with clasped hands looks straight up at the sky. The silver boiler, standing on a silver tripod above the fire, is kept alight by two multicoloured wooden figures, kneeling at either side of the boiler. One of them is blowing and the other is using a solid-silver pitchfork.  
The patrons of the altarpiece were a group of nuns devoted to St. John the Evangelist. There was another group of nuns in the same convent that devoted themselves to St. John the Baptist and commissioned a similar processional altar in honour of the saint. In fact, both altarpieces date from the beginning of the 18th century and were made in the same workshop. They both show the same crowned stamps of the city of Lisbon and the same maker's letter “M”.

2240cc1b-1ee5-59d4-b389-444e8504af89.short_description: The shape of the emerald at the centre of this pendant was determined by its crystallography, which is naturally hexagonal. At the bottom of the pendant are three gold loops, from which hang three teardrop-shaped emeralds.

233f177a-9a79-505a-9d9f-69315d5046d2.short_description:

None has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One who sustains and protects all that exists. Neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is he that intercedes with Him except with His Permission? He knows what happens to them (His creatures) in this world, and what will happen to them in the Hereafter. And they will never compass anything of his Knowledge except that which He wills. His *Kursi* (Chair) extends over the heavens and earth, and He feels no fatigue in guarding and preserving them".

2b78a938-ee55-5c81-860a-2ddf99017600.name: Bracelet
2b78a938-ee55-5c81-860a-2ddf99017600.short_description: This bracelet demonstrates the artistry and luxury of Islamic goldworking techniques in the Fatimid period. Fashioned from a This bracelet demonstrates the artistry and luxury of Islamic goldworking techniques in the Fatimid period. Fashioned from a single flat sheet of gold, the shank of the bracelet was decorated with repoussé and chased designs and then folded into a hollow tube; here the fine relief designs include human heads, birds, and harpies. The decoration of the elaborate circular clasp illustrates several complex techniques: twisted wire spirals, granulation and filigree. The stones are emeralds and rubies; the latter have been set with rock crystal, a favorite stone in the Fatimid period. Bracelets of this type were evidently made and worn in pairs, further magnifying the effect of the fine workmanship and precious materials. Such gold jewelry served not only as a spectacular form of personal adornment but also as an indicator of a woman’s wealth and social standing.
2b78a938-ee55-5c81-860a-2ddf99017600.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
2b78a938-ee55-5c81-860a-2ddf99017600.method_for_datation: The group of documents referred to as the Cairo Geniza is important to understanding the manufacture and circulation of jewelry in the Fatimid period. There, bracelets found in contemporaneous trousseau lists are described as *manfukh* (Arabic for “inflated” or “puffed up”), perhaps in reference to tubular or hollow bracelet such as this.
2b78a938-ee55-5c81-860a-2ddf99017600.method_for_provenance: The bracelet’s fine gold filigree work, granulation, and twisted wire spiral are all typical techniques of Fatimid jewelry.

32fdd8a2-bebf-5ad2-bcf2-45ef21b39556.name: Inkwell
32fdd8a2-bebf-5ad2-bcf2-45ef21b39556.short_description: This exquisite inkwell is an exceptional specimen of hardstone carving in medieval Islam. Contemporary accounts of minerals and semi-precious stones all refer to agate, which had been prized for small vessels since classical times but which, compared with rock crystal and jade, has barely survived. The faces of the inkwell bear the *basmala* and a Qur’anic inscription from *sura* *al-Kahf* (XVIII), verse 109, which is charmingly apposite. It reads: ‘If the ocean were ink (wherewith to write out) the words of my Lord, sooner would the ocean be exhausted than would the words of my Lord, even if we added another ocean like it, for its aid.’

388b0d1b-5233-57de-a649-d3f01bcaafa3.name: Lidded Jar
388b0d1b-5233-57de-a649-d3f01bcaafa3.description: This baluster-shaped pot is typical of imperial Mughal-style production. The decoration includes the traditional Kundan technique, where the stones are foil-backed and set into metal collets using high-carat gold foil, as opposed to being soldered. The technique dates back centuries in India but gained popularity during the Mughal period (AD 1526–1858), where today it remains the most popular method of setting stones. This lidded jar is decorated almost exclusively with green enamel in the champlevé technique, which etches the metal ground with fine lines before applying and fusing the enamel to the surface. Here, a series of fine lines can be seen through the translucent green enamel. The table-cut diamonds are arranged into six foliated panels set with floral sprays. The most unusual decorative feature is the green enamelled flower at the bottom of the base, detailed with petals ascending in size from the centre.

43a8c5d9-b3aa-529b-a3f9-5e64b5b32a48.name: The Pearl Carpet
43a8c5d9-b3aa-529b-a3f9-5e64b5b32a48.short_description: The foundation of silk and fine deer hide is densely embroidered overall with a design worked in strings of natural ‘Basra’ pearls, measuring approximately 1-3 mm, and English coloured glass beads. There are on average 78 pearls and beads per vertical dm. (10 cm), and 68 per horizontal dm., equaling a density of c.4,990 pearls and beads per dm2. The total area of the carpet is c. 45,670 cm2. The 32 smaller rosettes cover an area of c. 400 cm2 with smaller gems, and the total area embroidered with pearls and is beads is approximately 44,500 cm2. Therefore, over 2.2 million pearls and beads have been used to decorate the field. In our estimation, the number of pearls employed in the design is therefor at least 1.2-1.5 million.

4a08eb73-aef2-5e58-9066-f1c85dd23da4.name: Bracket Clock
4a08eb73-aef2-5e58-9066-f1c85dd23da4.description:
The case, made of gilt wood, has rich Rococo decoration. Its outline is composed of elongated C-scrolls primarily. The clock has a brass chapter ring with incised Roman numerals for the hours and Arabic numerals for minutes (at five-minute intervals). Semi-precious stones are applied at the outer edge of the chapter ring, at the centre of which is a small movable disc with alarm-setting marks from 1 to 12, and above it an aperture showing the control pendulum. All gaps as well as the arch of the dial have applied ornaments – C-scrolls, *rocaille* and leaves – made of silvered brass.  
The movement between plates is spring-driven with a verge escapement and a short pendulum. The hours, half and quarter hours are struck on bells. It has a separate alarm movement with a verge escapement and short pendulum.  
This clock is unusual for having above its main movement another, smaller one also with a verge escapement and pendulum. This served to drive the alarm and connected to the centre of the lower movement with a lever. It is wound up through the opening in the arch of the dial.  
The clock was in use in the Maruševec Manor near Varaždin. At the beginning of the 18th century Count Krsto Vragović owned the manor, he died in 1717 in a battle against the Turks. After that, Maruševec belonged to the Paszthory and Patačić families. In the 19th century, its owners were count Artur Schlippenbach and Oskar Pongratz.  
After the Second World War, the state confiscated the manor.

4c67ed2f-ee8b-5b76-827e-611ac07238ea.name: Pearl Trader’s Scales Box
4c67ed2f-ee8b-5b76-827e-611ac07238ea.short_description: This wooden box was designed to contain a sophisticated scales set, which incorporated both a large balance and bowls for weighing quantities of pearls and a smaller version, with several, graded weighing bowls for smaller quantities. The weighing systems for pearls was complex and highly sophisticated to allow for the accurate assessment of mixed batches of pearls of varying sizes and quality. The largest and most valuable pearls were separated and assessed individually. The other pearls would be passed through graded sieves and separated into three batches of specific size.  Apart from the very best items, pearls from these batches were sold by weight.

56bae231-ad09-5568-8e83-1f1aa7115444.name: Buckles (*Pafti*)
56bae231-ad09-5568-8e83-1f1aa7115444.short_description: Buckles were distinctive articles of adornment used throughout the centuries by Macedonian women. They were the most frequently worn and most exquisite articles of adornment in Macedonian women’s folk attire. Buckles used to be adorned with stylized geometric and floral patterns, the artistic effect having been emphasized by the application of decorative stones, filigree ornaments, gold-plating, pearls, mother-of-pearl, corals, chains and other embellishments. This outstanding set of buckles in leaf shapes is decorated with pearls and semi-precious stones, by application of the technique of "live" gold-plating.

5759f401-121f-5cef-8f4b-62d3d8fa9962.name: Spoon

701d0273-bf02-5200-8f32-6dab9287106b.short_description: The influences of Eastern art in Macedonia were largely expressed in the jewellery of the 19th century through the so-called Levantine Baroque style. 730d8f3c-b36e-5edb-a16b-a8c763ab2ca1.name: Order of the Osmanie that belonged to Alexandru Ioan Cuza
730d8f3c-b36e-5edb-a16b-a8c763ab2ca1.short_description: Alexandru Ioan Cuza, ruler of the United Principalities of Moldova and Wallachia, received the order of Osmanie in June 1864, when he travelled to Istanbul in order to convince the sultan to agree with the changes he planned to make to the Paris Convention of 1858, which was the Principalities’ constitution. In May the modified act was approved by plebiscite in the Principalities and as a consequence a conference of the Guaranteeing Powers was organized in Istanbul. Cuza spent two weeks in Istanbul and had talks with the sultan and the ambassadors of the Guaranteeing Powers. He managed to achieve his goal since on 28 June, the representatives of the Ottoman Empire, France, Great Britain, Prussia, Russia and Sardinia authorized *The Additional Act to the 1858 Convention*.

79123b79-bd2b-5af1-8898-89d1cb8e5327.name: Throne of Sultan Ahmed I.
79123b79-bd2b-5af1-8898-89d1cb8e5327.description:
The throne of Sultan Ahmed I is one of the best examples of 11th / 17th century Ottoman woodwork. Made in the form of a baldachin, the throne has three low steps that lead up to the one-person seat. The baldachin itself is crowned with a dome.  
  
The throne was made by the important 11th- / 17th-century architect Sedefkâr Mehmed Agha, the head architect of the Ottoman palace; it is dazzlingly beautiful with a mosaic of superb mother-of-pearl and tortoiseshell work side by side with countless precious gems.  
  
The throne is made of walnut wood. Its entire surface is decorated with a mosaic of mother-of-pearl and tortoiseshell. The vegetal decoration includes tulips, carnations, roses and peonies connected to each other by scrolling tendrils and rising from a vase. The vegetal motifs are executed in a naturalistic style in mother-of-pearl, while the remaining area is covered with tortoiseshell.  
  
The inner part of the seat of the throne is decorated with a composition of motifs in a lacquer technique known as *Edirnekari*. Floral motifs in yellow are painted against a red background in the naturalistic style.  
  
The floral motifs which reflect the characteristic style of the Classical Ottoman period are arranged in a most successful composition. The vase and the flowers themselves are further enlivened by the addition of precious gems, including emeralds, jade, turquoise, and diamonds. The use of precious gems in various colours makes the throne even more attractive.  
  
The throne is one of many objects which display the wealth of the Ottoman Palace. It is an important example of the high level of quality attained in vegetal decoration in 11th / 17th century Ottoman art.

7b5dfa6d-5872-5368-aeb3-65783684e2ef.name: Pearl Grading Sieves
7b5dfa6d-5872-5368-aeb3-65783684e2ef.short_description: These copper alloy sieves were used to grade pearls into their various sizes. The larger, heavier and more luminous a pearl was, the higher its price.These pearl sieves were known as tus or tasat (sing. Tasa). Carefully graded, they are deep circular vessels, their bases pierced and designed to fit one into the other. According to local sources, sets could consists of between four and 45 units. Traditionally, these pearl sieves were used by the tawwash or sea-going merchant, who carried them in a characteristic cloth bag or dasta, when he visited the pearlers, together with all the other implements of his trade, i.e. portable scales and agate weights, a pearl scoop, and his table for calculating the value of the pearls.

7ec5b54e-b5f6-55dc-bba6-dbab52faa88a.name: Yataghan from the court of Süleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520–66)
7ec5b54e-b5f6-55dc-bba6-dbab52faa88a.short_description: The exquisite workmanship and lavish use of precious materials employed in this sword’s construction exemplifies the opulence and refinement of Ottoman luxury arts. It is almost certainly from the same imperial workshop as a nearly identical *yataghan* produced in 1526–27 by the court jeweller Ahmed Tekel for the Ottoman sultan Süleyman the Magnificent (r. 1520–66). The gold incrustation on the blade depicts a combat between a dragon and a phoenix against a background of foliate scrolls. These figures, like the gold-inlaid cloud bands and foliate scrolls on the ivory grips, are Chinese in inspiration, and were probably introduced into Ottoman art through contacts with Persia.

7fd24a74-b039-5ba4-b6a9-6fe4522c585f.name: Gold necklace.
7fd24a74-b039-5ba4-b6a9-6fe4522c585f.description:
A gold necklace decorated with exquisitely interwoven ornamentation, which assumes the form of intertwined vegetal boughs. The necklace is composed of two chains joined to 20 *sumluks* (an oval shaped ornamental unit), which are decorated with interwoven vegetal tendrils. Tiny blossoms are suspended from 16 *sumluks,* each of which ends in a pearl-drop. A pendant in the shape of an inverted crescent hangs down from the two central *sumluks*; the pendant is stamped with an inscription written in *naskhi* script and coloured enamel, which reads: 'Eternal Glory'. A circular medallion with a large carnelian lobe in its centre is suspended from the pendant. On the left and right of the pendant, are two other pendants (suspended from two *sumluks)*, the centres of which are adorned by a lobe from the 'bloodstone' – a type of carnelian agate.  
Muslim craftsman used a number of techniques to decorate jewellery, including inlay with precious gems and enamel, high- and low-relief carving, filigree, latticework and incising. In the decoration of this piece, the art of interweaving or latticework was used, which involved the preparation of gold to form long wires that were then shaped into decorative intertwining forms connected together by specialised welding.
7fd24a74-b039-5ba4-b6a9-6fe4522c585f.short_description: This richly decorated necklace studded with precious stones may have belonged to a princess.
7fd24a74-b039-5ba4-b6a9-6fe4522c585f.dates: Approximately hegira mid-7th century / AD 13th century.
7fd24a74-b039-5ba4-b6a9-6fe4522c585f.method_for_datation: The necklace was dated based on an analysis of the type and style of decoration used; in view of the fact that intertwined and interwoven vegetal stems are considered as part of the ornamental vocabulary that was widespread during the Ayyubid era, and that the motif appeared on a number of buildings as well as other applied objects. In addition, the expression: 'Eternal Glory', which was written on one of the necklace's suspended pendants, has connections with literature of the Ayyubid period.
7fd24a74-b039-5ba4-b6a9-6fe4522c585f.obtention: This piece was bought from a dealer of antiquities, Fu'ad Bulus, in 1937.

8bd10ee7-7d61-5332-9316-61a61303f68d.name: Heart-shaped amulet with Sura
8bd10ee7-7d61-5332-9316-61a61303f68d.short_description: An amulet made of white and red garnet in the shape of a heart. In the centre there is an inscription in *naskhi* epigraphy reading: "Thunder (Ar-Ra'ad) glorifies and praises Him, and so do the angels because of His Awe", and is surrounded with *Ayat-al-Kursi* (*The Chair*) in *naskhi*, reading: "Allah! none has the right to be worshipped but He, the Ever Living, the One who sustains and protects all that exists. Neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth. Who is he that intercedes with Him except with His Permission? He knows what happens to them (His creatures) in this world, and what will happen to them in the Hereafter. And they will never compass anything of his Knowledge except that which He wills. His *Kursi* (Chair) extends over the heavens and earth, and He feels no fatigue in guarding and preserving them. And He is the most High, the most Great". The amulet is framed by two lines.

8c623df6-63e7-59cd-8751-f117d02f1259.name: Necklace
8c623df6-63e7-59cd-8751-f117d02f1259.short_description: This necklace comprised of ten turquoise stones which are fashioned into oval and polygonal shapes. The turquoise stones are connected using enamelled gold rosette spacers. The inscriptions and decorated foliate motifs on the turquoise stones are inlaid with gold. The *nasta’liq* inscriptions recall popular devotional phrases dedicated to a special and important individual. Turquoise or *firuzeh* which means victory is a national colour in Iran. It was the preferred colour of the interior and exterior of domed mosques, as it symbolises the heavens.

91a520f6-9937-54cd-a224-0a3b83e3587f.name: Azurite
91a520f6-9937-54cd-a224-0a3b83e3587f.short_description: Two aggregates of azurite prismatic crystals with a radial distribution. Azurite is a copper carbonate mineral, of chemical formula Cu3(CO3)2(OH)2. Its name comes from the antiquity for its deep blue colour after the Arabian azure that came from the Persian lazhward. Azurite crystals conform to the monoclinic system of symmetry. In this sample they are prismatic, opaque and their faces present striations. The lustre is vitreous. Azurite was used as a blue pigment for centuries, providing a wide range of blues. It is also used as jewellery and as an ornamental stone. As a secondary mineral found in the oxidized portions of copper deposits, the presence of Azurite is a good surface indicator of the presence of copper ores. This sample was collected at the Touissit Mine, near Oudja, Morocco.

92830f7a-b5c3-5e7e-9a7f-a0686de50300.name: *Peškun*
92830f7a-b5c3-5e7e-9a7f-a0686de50300.description:
This *Peškun* (Tr. *peşkun*) has a base of ten vertical sides that carry a protruding decagonal plate at the top. The sides are also divided horizontally into three zones, the highest of which has a central flower motif, the middle a honeycomb-like openwork ellipse, and the lowest an opening in the form of a pointed five-leafed arch, below which is a flower with leaves and a rounded three-leafed arch. On the upper panel, there is a star-shaped field with a flower in the center of it, while other floral motifs are in the spaces between the decagon and the arms of the star. All floral and geometric ornaments are made of mother-of-pearl and brass wire using the incrustation technique, while the edge of the decagonal top plate is ornamented with bone.  
*Peškun* is the name of a traditional piece of Ottoman furniture in the shape of a table or stool. It was originally meant for sitting, although it had different purposes throughout history, especially as a decorative table in Balkan oriental interiors of the 19th and of the first half of the 20th century. Over time, the larger table (in the set of usually three pieces) began to be used as a coffee table, while the smaller ones were used as stools. *Peškun* were ordinarily made of walnut wood, ornamented with incrusted floral and geometric motifs made of mother-of-pearl and bone.

939c981d-a3af-5e38-a3ec-2694fa181d2b.name: Priming Flask
939c981d-a3af-5e38-a3ec-2694fa181d2b.short_description: This exceptionally well-crafted primer (powder flask) was probably made in an imperial Mughal workshop. Carved in a somewhat hemispherical shape, with a short, integral spout and large flattened base, the entire centre was masterfully hollowed out through a single, small round opening. After drilling and abrading to form the flask’s shape, the delicate floral patterning was then carved in low relief, with rounded petals, subtle veins and a crosshatch pattern in the central spray all detailed.

9f6f6d17-a330-58b4-8043-735c770a690a.name: Dagger (*Kard*)
9f6f6d17-a330-58b4-8043-735c770a690a.short_description: This outstanding dagger with its lapis-lazuli hilt has a deeply engraved calligraphic inscription on its blade that is compartmentalised within a continous arabesque scroll. The calligraphy reads “Ya Muhammad, Ya ‘Ali” alternatively. The quality of the blade indicates a royal commission and an experienced metal smith. The dagger is signed on its spine with the attribute name of Ghulam Shah ‘Abbasi, in gold damascened foliage. The attribution ‘Ghulam Shah ‘Abbasi or ‘Slave of Shah ‘Abbasi’ indicates a period in Iranian history when Nadir Shah rose to power and deposed the last members of the Safavid dynasty.

a5b2538f-6e41-5940-b65c-59d0b57a7466.name: Necklace (*lebba*).
a5b2538f-6e41-5940-b65c-59d0b57a7466.description: This large necklace consists of several pendants alternating with fluted ovoid gold pearls on a silk cord. The pendants consist of different golden drops in the shape of fleurons or roses of Rhodes known as *gharnati*, rosettes, crescent moons and stars that come together to form a long broad necklace covering almost the entire chest. The pendants are decorated on both sides, each studded with ten emeralds and garnets on one side and decorated on the other with green, red and blue champlevé enamel with floral and plant decoration. This type of jewellery was worn by brides from Fez on their wedding day and by upper-middle-class women during festivities. The magic symbols that they bear are intended to protect the women against the evil eye. The fact that there are ten precious stones (twice five, the symbol of the hand that protects from harm) and the crescent-and-moon motif, imitating an eyebrow and an iris (the eye that sees danger) indicate the importance that women placed on amulets.
a5b2538f-6e41-5940-b65c-59d0b57a7466.short_description: This necklace, consisting of several pendants decorated on both sides, would have been worn by a bride. It includes symbols intended to protect her against bad luck: the two hands represented by the ten precious stones set in medallions, and the eye represented by the crescent and the circle.

b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.name: Monstrance of the Bemposta
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.alternate_name: Monstrance of the Chapel of the Palace of Bemposta or Palace of the Queen
b2ca91ca-c46b-5e08-b073-5f3ded54c993.description:
This magnificent monstrance in gilded silver and gold with a triangular base, sits on three volutes ornamented with floral motifs, ribbons and cartouches. On the three inferior angles of the base there are cherubs and three figures that symbolise Faith, Hope and Charity. On the top corners there are three full-bodied angels conveying Eucharistic motifs, while six cherubs and seraphs, overlap, ascending along the stem.  
On the three faces of the base oval bas-reliefs represent themes from the Eucharist: The Supper at Emmaus and the giant bunch of grapes, Fruit from the Promised Land and Christ at Calvary.  
The monstrance' sunburst is encircled by clouds. It has a radiant splendor with irregular rays, covered with precious stones. The monstrance's surface is entirely adorned with precious stones, some of them large and of excellent quality, creating a spectacular decorative and chromatic effect.  
The theatrical splendor of the Baroque is well illustrated through the use of jewels and quality chiselling, admirably assembled in a dazzling combination of metal and gemstones.  
It is likely the monstrance was commissioned by King Pedro III, husband of Queen Maria I. In Pedro III's Will of 1786 he foresees that his son, the future King João VI, should have the country house in Queluz, and urges him to care for the divine cult traditionally associated with the Bemposta Chapel, where he wished the precious monstrance to be kept.  
Attribution of this piece is controversial. Traditionally, researchers attributed it to J. F. Ludovice, the goldsmith and architect of the Convent of Mafra. Their theories were based on an existing drawing of the monstrance at the Museum, which also came from the Bemposta Palace.

baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.name: Breast Ornament
baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.description:
Jewellery reached its zenith in the 18th century. Monarchs throughout Europe – from Lisbon to Dresden; England to Naples – wore jewellery to reinforce their majesty and political power. High standards of craftsmanship together with up-to-date designs supplied the luxurious and ostentatious Portuguese court of Kings João V (1706–1750) , José I (1750–1777) and Queen D. Maria I.  
At this time of Portuguese Absolutism, the magnificence of Portuguese jewellery is closely linked with the colonisation of Brazil, with enormous quantities of gold pouring into the kingdom (from 1699) and diamonds (from 1729) onwards. Greater quantities of precious gems were mined in Brazil, in Rio das Velhas, Minas Gerais, Mato Grosso and Bahía, further increasing the materials available.  
This particular ornamental breast jewellery – which would have adorned a lady's dress – is a remarkable example from the period. So many bejewelled women would have added to the splendour of court life, its balls and receptions. The naturalism of this piece together with the asymmetrical composition confirms that the fashions emanating from the French court of Louis XV were extremely popular, although from the late 1760s this gave way to the Rococo style exemplified by softer and more graceful shapes of exceptional beauty.  
This piece of jewellery was designed as a single piece with the exception of the garland topping it which was added later. Ornaments such as this one were often constructed in stand-alone parts so they could be worn separately. The silver structure is set with chrysoberyls, garnets, yellow topazes, colourless gem-stones quartz, beryl and topaz. The array of colourful gems includes green and blue doublets and, as usual then, a fair number of quartz and topaz backed with various shades of coloured foil to create striking variations of light and colour.
baeb2f18-d363-5177-9890-45fa4c7ce945.short_description: Costume jewellery of this kind was a magnificent addition to a lady’s dress. Typologically it relates to the fashionable aristocratic jewellery of the European courts from the second half of the 18th century. It is also a direct consequence of the Portuguese colonisation of Brazil.

bb98e522-f646-5d72-a9f4-01e1cce27fbd.name: Brooch (Amulet)
bb98e522-f646-5d72-a9f4-01e1cce27fbd.short_description: Originally a heart-shaped amulet with a longitudinal perforation at the top which allowed it to be strung and hung. It was later set in a gold-and-enamel mount, fitted with a clasp, and served as a brooch. The stone features engraved and gilded Arabic inscriptions in *naskhi* and in *nasta'liq* script; there are also several inscriptions in low relief. The texts along the border reproduce in their entirety four of the last Suras, starting at the top, from right to left, as follows: Sura CIX (*Al Kafirun* / *The Disbelievers*), Sura CXII (*Al Ikhlas* / *Sincerity*), Sura CXIV (*Al Nas* / *Mankind*), and Sura CXIII (*Al Falaq* / *The Daybreak*). Other inscriptions are incorporated into a vegetal design whose large leaves are used as epigraphic cartouches. At the bottom, the invocation ‘*Ya ‘Ali!*’ (‘O ‘Ali!’). The texts are either excerpts from the Qur’an, such as verse 13 from Sura XIII (*Al Ra’d* / *The Thunder*) and verse 13 from Sura LXI (*Al Saff* / *The Ranks*), or formulas exalting the divine power and invocations which include several of the ninety-nine names of Allah. Also inscribed on the stone are the Muslim profession of faith, *shahada* (‘there is no god but Allah, and Muhammad is the messenger of Allah’), and the invocation ‘*Ya Muhammad!*’ (‘O Muhammad!’).

bd425b9a-5df3-53ae-8d59-3df33045cb72.name: Pair of fibulae.
bd425b9a-5df3-53ae-8d59-3df33045cb72.description:
Each of the two fibulae consists of a sliding tongue on an arch and a decorative body finished on the edge opposite the pin with a small ring intended to fix the chain that joined the two fibulae. The body of the fibula is ovoid and its decoration arranged radially. Four bezels in the shape of fleurons known as *gharnati* or roses of Rhodes set with two green fluorite stones and two garnets emanate from an oval medallion studded with a green fluorite stone. Foliate compositions consisting of double grooved palms and three symmetrical palms in the shape of fleurons also emerge from the centre. These are decorated with baroque pearls attached to the surface of the piece with gold wire fixed with a small golden ball. The edges of the fibula are decorated with double palms whose lobes curl in different directions to form a line of festoons.  
This valuable, practical piece of jewellery was intended to hold up the bride's *haik* (robe) and includes a prophylactic symbol against the evil eye. In fact, the cruciform arrangement consisting of five stones suggests the five-fingered hand motif as well as the central eye that sees danger and scatters it to the four winds to protect the new bride or wife who wears it from any misfortune that the envious may wish upon her.
bd425b9a-5df3-53ae-8d59-3df33045cb72.short_description: These fibulae have sliding pin, semi-circular fastenings and were used to fix a bride's dress. These are coupled with a plaque decorated on both sides to complete the piece. One side is enamelled and the other studded with five precious stones, the symbol of the hand.

bd7a3cd3-6bbf-5036-bebe-7fdc38ffd56d.name: Monstrance
bd7a3cd3-6bbf-5036-bebe-7fdc38ffd56d.description:
The monstrance is by the Graz goldsmith, Hans Georg Pfisterer. The shaped oval base has enamel medallions showing scenes from the Passion of Christ and continues into a knob, shaped like a Baroque vase, from which rises the top part of the monstrance of the so-called sun type. Bands and foliate ornaments completely cover it intertwined with filigree and jewels. The opening of the ostensory has a six-sided moulded frame made up of wavy and angled sides and surrounded by airy filigree ornamentation of entwined scrolls and jewels that form flowers. Above the ostensory is a richly decorated canopy under which God the Father, holding the globe, hovers in clouds. Above the canopy is the dove of the Holy Ghost. At the foot of the frame, two adoring angels kneel on narrow decorated bases. The bottom edge of the monstrance has a lambrequin motif from which pearls hang.  
Bishop Juraj Branjug of Zagreb acquired the monstrance. He was one of Croatia’s most active bishops in 18th-century in the field of religious art building a new palace in Zagreb and renovating and building many churches. He had his own woodcarving workshop at Kaptol whose master craftsmen made altarpieces and pulpits adorned with the bishop’s arms for many churches. He bought and donated first-class liturgical objects to the cathedral.

Made by the Graz goldsmith, Georg Pfisterer, it was acquired by Bishop Juraj Branjug for Zagreb Cathedral.

ca59fd60-c057-5dbf-a2fa-484dcab24b97.short_description: Thin silver ring with oval-shaped agate stone set in silver with inherent decoration on the soundings. Silver jewellery was the most common, because only rich people could afford gold jewellery. The Jordanian economy relied on trades and crafts and new waves of people started to come to Jordan and began to settle for this purpose. This object is an example of how traditional fashion reflected the variegated population composition of Jordan in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. It is also an example of local personal attire, fashion, costumes and rites.

cfe5bd9c-e197-550b-b7be-fc5f83730d8f.name: One of a pair of earrings.
cfe5bd9c-e197-550b-b7be-fc5f83730d8f.description:
Gold manufacturing has been known in Syria from at least 2000 BC. Gold artefacts, moulds, and various goldsmiths' tools have been found in numerous Syrian archaeological sites, including those at Ugarit, Mushrifa, and Ebla. During the Classical period, gold jewellery was widely produced in Syria, particularly in Hawran, Palmyra (Tadmur) and Homs.  
The development of gold manufacturing in Syria continued during the Islamic period, as exemplified by surviving examples such as this single earring, made from woven gold in the form of a circular disk with radiating edges lined by a string of pearls. In the centre of the disc is a triangular formation of two red rubies and a green emerald. A circular ruby instead of a pearl indicates the top side of the disc, out of which protrudes a link to another triangular set of three precious stones mirroring the ones on the filigree disk, a green emerald and two red rubies set within gold mounts. Above them, located near the ear wire, is a final decorative feature of a little pierced golden sphere also containing a precious stone; an emerald.
cfe5bd9c-e197-550b-b7be-fc5f83730d8f.short_description: This gold filigree earring encrusted with precious emeralds, rubies and pearls indicates the high quality of jewellery production for which the Fatimid period is famed. Similar finds from Egypt and Syria abound.
cfe5bd9c-e197-550b-b7be-fc5f83730d8f.method_for_datation: The production of highly refined gold jewellery flourished in Egypt and Syria during the Fatimid period (358–567 / AD 969–1171). The techniques employed included filigree and a method using granules of gold; twisted rope-like gold, and occasionally inlay work with gems were also employed. Products include bracelets, armlets, earrings, pendants, rings, belts, brooches, and hair ornaments.
cfe5bd9c-e197-550b-b7be-fc5f83730d8f.method_for_provenance: During the Fatimid period, the gold-production centres of Syria and Egypt flourished, particularly those in Aleppo and Cairo. Although this item was obtained by the Museum from Raqqa, it is not possible to determine the provenance of this object definitively.

e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.name: Monstrance of the Golden Sun of Moravia
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.description:
This vessel, used for carrying the Host – the embodiment of Christ's flesh – the presentation of which constitutes the spiritual climax of a mass, is one of the most precious specimens of the goldsmith's craft in Moravia. An oval incised base supports a vase-like *nodus* bearing a sunburst with an aperture lined with a cartouche, accentuated by a crest motif. The typically Baroque, intricately undulating ornamentation with faggoting encircles a case with a lunette, a crescent for holding the Host.  
The sun as the source of life, light and Divine truth lent its name to a whole group of “solar” monstrances contrasting with medieval monstrances which were spire-shaped with Gothic pinnacles.  
The decoration features certain older elements originally associated with objects now lost. The most interesting of them is an enamel label set into the back of the monstrance leg. It depicts St. Wenceslas on a Gothic throne – the emblem of the Olomouc Chapter – with the coats-of-arms of Emperor Ferdinand III (1637–1662), brother of Leopold I Vilém of Habsburg, Bishop of Olomouc and Archduke of Austria. The Gothic-style throne in the chapter emblem, supplemented with Dietrichstein wine-maker knives, possibly represents the actual “throne of St. Wenceslas” in the Olomouc cathedral, commissioned by Bishop František of Dietrichstein.  
The origin of the monstrance was once associated with Cardinal Wolfgang Hanibal of Schrattenbach, Bishop of Olomouc, who bequeathed a significant amount of money for its creation. In fact, the monstrance was commissioned by the Olomouc Chapter, headed by Dean Kašpar Florentin of Glandorf and Canon Jiří Jindrich Mayer of Mayerswald, who also commissioned a missal decorated with wrought silver (1733). In recognition of its high artistic value, the monstrance remained Chapter property even after an imperial decree issued after the Napoleonic wars ordered that all objects with precious stones be transferred to Vienna.
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.short_description: This vessel, for carrying the Host, the embodiment of Christ's flesh, is one of only a few gold monstrances in Europe. The typically baroque, intricately undulating ornamentation encircles a case with a lunette, the crescent for holding the Host. The sunburst symbolises the source of life, light and Divine truth.
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.method_for_datation: Marked with hallmarks, it is the only known work by a Brno goldsmith demonstrating close contacts between Brno and Olomouc, the two main centres of Moravia. Although goldsmiths of the same name were also active in Augsburg and Linz, their family ties have not yet been proven.
e07117dd-950e-5f5f-9ae1-7e9e6b78feb2.obtention: Following extensive restoration, the monstrance, from the treasury of the Cathedral of St. Wenceslas Olomouc, is exhibited at the Archdiocesan Museum, Olomouc.

e0dd9b89-fd8e-5b2e-a57e-fda48b2a6792.name: *Peškun*
e0dd9b89-fd8e-5b2e-a57e-fda48b2a6792.description: Оctagonal *peškun* (Tr. *peşkun*) decorated with floral and geometric motifs, each side having a blossom branch ornament that rests on a pointed draped arch at the bottom spreading to the top of a side. A heart-shaped branch has a flower at the top, while its bottom makes a central part of an opening in the shape of braces. The leaves surround the branch and are placed in a horizontal rectangular field at the top of the side as well. Eight sides carry an octagonal plate at the top with a central flower and floral motifs that surround it. The inner octagonal of the plate’s edge is decorated with leaves. All ornaments are made of mother-of-pearl and brass wire using the incrustation technique, while the edge of the octagonal top plate is ornamented with bone. Peškun is the name of a traditional piece of Ottoman furniture in the shape of a table or stool, originally meant for sitting, although it had different purposes throughout history, especially as a decorative table in Balkan oriental interiors of the 19th and of the first half of the 20th century. Over time, the larger table in the set (of usually three pieces) began to be used as a coffee table, while the smaller ones were used as stools. The *Peškun* was ordinarily made of walnut wood, ornamented with incrusted floral and geometric motifs made of mother of pearl and bone.

e41aaf26-c6bd-574f-9c43-894434363d66.name: Order of the lion and the Sun, presented to Sir John Kinneir MacDonald, the East India Company’s envoy to Iran (1824–30)
e41aaf26-c6bd-574f-9c43-894434363d66.short_description:
In 1807, under European influence and modelled on the Légion d’Honneur, Fath ‘Ali Shah instituted The Order of the Sun, which he awarded to the French ambassador General Claude Mathieu Gardane. In 1809 the British envoy Sir Harford Jones refused to be awarded with the same insignia because of the hostilities with the French. As a consequence, in 1810, Fath ‘Ali Shah modified the Order of the Sun and created the new Order of the Lion and Sun, which was presented to John Malcolm, the envoy of the East India Company. The Khalili Order of the Lion and Sun was awarded by Fath ‘Ali Shah to Sir John Kinneir MacDonald (1782–1830), the East India Company’s envoy to Iran from 1824 to 1830, for his commitment in arranging a peace treaty with Russia. The insignia consists of a plaque, a collar and a star.  
The plaque, which is decorated with a crouching lion-and-sun, bears the signature of Muhammad Ja‘far, a leading artist in painted enamels at the Qajar court, and the date AH 1242 (AD 1826–7). The collar consists of a double chain with eight enamelled plaques, eight small rosettes, the ‘Kayanid’ crown and a pendant. The star is decorated with an enamelled circular panel with the lion-and-sun and surrounded by a large number of facet-cut diamonds, emeralds and spinels.

e55614b8-f79a-5fa9-af73-256d887343b2.name: Pectoral plate
e55614b8-f79a-5fa9-af73-256d887343b2.short_description: Besides the obvious decorative purposes, jewellery in such heavily tribal societies indicates ethnic identity and social status. Turkoman jewellery is usually gilded; both gold and brass were used. Carnelian is the stone of choice used for inlay. It is believed to protect the wearer from death and sickness besides bringing happiness and peace. Amuletic jewellery, called *tumar*, is worn among all Turkoman tribes. *Tumar*s are classified as pectorals as they are worn around the neck and fall over the chest, although they can reach as far as the waist. This large silver pectoral features a double-headed bird, which since ancient times has been a symbol of power and authority.

eb99c41a-8360-57b5-82cd-a9ebce2e752f.short_description: The upper portion of this South Indian pendant features two stylized peacocks facing a central rosette. The central flower has seven petals inset with diamonds surrounding a central emerald. The reverse of the pendant is plain gold (not covered in enamel) and includes several marks, possibly those of former owners. The rubies come from Myanmar (Burma), which has been known as a source of rubies to Europeans since the late fifteenth century.

fba06fef-805f-5de9-8213-221cfe8fe3db.name: Nephrite bowl with enamel picture
fba06fef-805f-5de9-8213-221cfe8fe3db.short_description: This bowl features the enamelled portrait of Fath-Ali Shah Qajar, emperor of Persia (AD 1797–1834); it is signed by the artist, Ghülam Khanetzad, and dated AH 1233. fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.name: Tomb
fd7ea3bd-87be-5e84-a68b-74d44c3f3fc9.description:
The tomb, which is made of gilded silver shaped like a reliquary, holds a casket within which a figurine of Christ lies. Resting upon a trilateral base and supported on the backs of three ivory dragons, the tomb is decorated with embossed and chased foliate and *rocaille* ornaments and jewels. Enamel tablets hold within them scenes from the Life of Christ. From the base, a halo rises surrounded by a border of double rays. Attached to the base are allegorical figures of Faith, Hope and Love, flanked by St. Peter and St. Paul, and above them the figures of the Fathers of the Church Saints Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome and Gregory. The centre of the sunburst halo holds an enamelled painting of the Virgin and Child in a jewelled frame. It is decorated with foliate and *rocaille* ornaments, supported by two gilded angels. Above the frame is a splendid jewelled crown with a pendant pearl, flanked by two small ivory angels.  
Made in Augsburg and bought for the treasury with money bequeathed by Cardinal Juraj Haulik (the first Archbishop of Zagreb enthroned in 1853) a great patron of the arts and patriot whose ideas reflected the Enlightenment spirit.
